passage: Himani, it's Sarita, and you're the first person I'm telling out loud. Last Tuesday I opened my phone and there was a message from a blank account: "I know your bus. Watch your back." My hands went cold. Part of me wanted to reply, to say something clever, to show I wasn't scared. But I did not. I took a screenshot of everything, blocked the account and sat there breathing. Then I walked into the kitchen and showed my father. He didn't panic. He called the school the next morning and they said we could file a report if it continued. I'm not saying it stopped my heart from racing. But I know now that this was never a game I had to win.

qa.q: What did the message on Sarita's phone say?
qa.a: It said, "I know your bus. Watch your back."

qa.q: Why did Sarita want to reply at first?
qa.a: She felt scared and wanted to look brave and clever, so part of her wanted to answer back. Her cold hands show real fear under that wish.

qa.q: What steps did Sarita take that protect her?
qa.a: She did not answer, took screenshots, blocked the account and showed her father, who called the school.

qa.q: How might her father have felt seeing the message?
qa.a: He likely felt worried and protective, but he stayed calm so Sarita could feel safe telling him.

grounding: A teenager treats an online threat seriously, avoids engaging, keeps a record and reports it.

passage: I'm the neighbour who walks his dog by the lane behind Nirmala's house, and I saw a bit of this last week. A boy from her school leaned on the wall and said something low to her. I couldn't hear it, but her shoulders went stiff and she walked on without turning. Later I saw her sitting on the step with her phone, typing and saving something. I can't say what she felt, she might have been scared, or just angry, or both. The next morning she was walking to the bus with her mother, who had a folder in her hand. I mentioned what I'd seen to her mother, in case it helped. Gurpreet.

qa.q: Where did the narrator see the boy speak to Nirmala?
qa.a: He saw it in the lane behind Nirmala's house.

qa.q: What might Nirmala's stiff shoulders and silence suggest?
qa.a: They may suggest fear or anger, and Gurpreet says he cannot be certain of what she felt. Walking on without answering fits a wish to avoid engaging.

qa.q: What would you advise Nirmala to do?
qa.a: Keep a record of what was said, tell her mother, school or authorities, and avoid answering him.

qa.q: How might Nirmala's mother feel on hearing what the neighbour saw?
qa.a: She may feel worried but glad someone spoke up, since it supports the report she is making.

grounding: A teen takes an in-person threat seriously, avoids engaging, records it and tells a trusted adult, seen by an observer.

passage: I sit in the third row and saw Irfan debate whether uniforms should be compulsory. He opened with a survey the class had run, twenty-two out of thirty who said comfort mattered more. Then Zoya from the other team made the point that uniforms reduce pressure to compete with clothes, and Irfan paused. He said, "That's fair, I hadn't looked at it that way. But I'd still argue that a few casual days would keep the benefit." He didn't shout. His voice stayed level while his foot tapped. The other side actually nodded at him. Whether he changed his own mind, I can't say. But he sounded like he was listening, and he still held his ground. Abhinav.

qa.q: What did Irfan open his debate with?
qa.a: He opened with a survey the class had run.

qa.q: What might Irfan's tapping foot and level voice suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he felt some nervous energy but was managing it, since his voice stayed level. Abhinav says he can't tell whether Irfan changed his mind.

qa.q: What did Irfan do that strengthened his argument?
qa.a: He acknowledged Zoya's good point and then defended his own view with a specific proposal.

qa.q: How might the other team have felt about being acknowledged?
qa.a: They probably felt heard and respected, which is why they nodded at him.

grounding: A teen builds an argument with evidence, acknowledges a good point and defends a view, seen by an observer.

passage:
Monday. In the family debate about homework hours, Bhupen talked over everyone and called his sister Alka's point "stupid". She stopped speaking. He won the shouting and lost the room.
Wednesday. Bhupen asked his teacher for two studies on sleep and school. He wrote three points down and one thing Alka might say back.
Saturday. At dinner he said, "Alka, you were right that some homework builds habits. I'd like to argue that shorter tasks work as well, and here's a study." Alka leaned forward. "Okay, show me." They spent an hour going through it. Nobody won, but Papa said it was the best conversation they'd had in months.

qa.q: What did Bhupen call Alka's point on Monday?
qa.a: He called it "stupid".

qa.q: Why did Bhupen prepare a point Alka might say back?
qa.a: He probably wanted to understand her view and not lose the room again, so he expected her counterpoint. It suggests he now cares about being fair as well as being right.

qa.q: What made the Saturday debate go better than Monday's?
qa.a: He used evidence, admitted a good point from Alka and stayed respectful instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt on Monday?
qa.a: She probably felt dismissed and silenced, which is why she stopped speaking.

grounding: A teen learns that debate skill includes evidence and acknowledging good points, and that ridicule and volume fail.

passage: I watched my cousin Zubin bargain with his mother about phone time last Sunday, and I was surprised because he stayed calm. Last month he used to argue until doors banged. This time he said, "Amma, can we try an hour of phone after homework for two weeks? If I keep my marks up and you see me put it away at nine, we can talk about more." His mother looked at him a long moment. "Two weeks," she said. "Show me." He did not sulk or promise the moon. I can't tell what he felt, maybe nervous, maybe just tired of fighting. Later he told me it felt good to be trusted a little. Ritu.

qa.q: What did Zubin ask his mother for?
qa.a: He asked to try an hour of phone after homework for two weeks.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been feeling as he made his proposal?
qa.a: He may have felt nervous and hopeful, and perhaps tired of arguing. Ritu admits she cannot be certain, since he stayed calm on the outside.

qa.q: What made Zubin's approach more likely to succeed?
qa.a: He offered trust-building steps and a trial period, instead of arguing or demanding.

qa.q: How might Zubin's mother have felt hearing it?
qa.a: She may have felt reassured that he was thinking about responsibility, while still wanting to see it work. 🙂

grounding: A teen bargains calmly for phone time with a trial period, seen by an observer.

passage:
Friday. Afreen wanted to stay out until ten for her friend's engagement dinner and argued with her father, Jagdish, for twenty minutes. He said no, she stormed off. 
Sunday. She wrote out a plan: the venue, who would drive her home, a message every hour, and "if I break any of it, I'll go back to nine." She left it by his tea.
Thursday. Jagdish said, "We'll try ten for this dinner only." Afreen said thank you and kept every promise. A few weeks later, when she asked for another late evening, he said yes before she'd finished asking.

qa.q: What did Afreen leave by her father's tea?
qa.a: She left a written plan by his tea.

qa.q: Why did Afreen write out a plan instead of arguing again?
qa.a: She probably realised that arguing had not worked, and she wanted to show him she could be trusted. Writing it also gave her a calmer way to ask.

qa.q: What did the trial arrangement do for the family?
qa.a: It gave Jagdish a way to say yes safely, and gave Afreen a chance to prove herself.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt on Friday?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and firm, and perhaps annoyed by the argument, since he said no and she stormed off.

grounding: A teen negotiates curfew with a written plan and a trial period, across several days.

passage:
Saturday night.

Hansa and the boys from the next lane wanted me to ride over the old railway bridge on our cycles, no helmets, in the dark, "just for a laugh". Hansa kept saying, "Everyone's coming, Santosh, don't be boring." My stomach felt tight. I said, "No, I'm out. But I'll do the kite competition instead, tomorrow morning, if you all come." Hansa said, "Fine," but he sulked. One of the others said, "Why not? Are you scared?" I said, "Yes, a bit. And Papa would ground me."

It felt strange to say. They went without me. I felt lonely for an hour and relieved for the rest of the night. Sunday, 7 am. Hansa turned up for the kites. 🙂

qa.q: What did the boys want Santosh to ride over?
qa.a: They wanted him to ride over the old railway bridge.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when the boys pressed him?
qa.a: His stomach felt tight, so he was nervous and scared, and after refusing he felt lonely and then relieved. He also admitted being a bit scared.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that a good friend could accept?
qa.a: He said no clearly, blamed his father's rule and suggested a safer plan, the kite competition.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Santosh refused?
qa.a: He may have felt disappointed and a bit embarrassed at being turned down, which could explain the sulk, but he still came to the kites.

grounding: A teen faces persuasion to try something risky and says no, suggests another plan and blames a rule.

passage: Wasim, I'll tell you what happened, but don't laugh. Last month I got into a mess. A boy from Class Eleven kept following me home and asking for money, and I gave him some twice because I was scared. I told nobody for three weeks. Then one night I couldn't sleep and I went to Papa's room. My heart was thumping. I expected shouting, and I already had my excuse ready. Instead he sat up, listened without stopping me and said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's think about what to do." He didn't punish me for giving the money. We went to the school together next morning. I still feel nervous, but I don't feel alone. Suraj.

qa.q: How long did Suraj tell nobody?
qa.a: He told nobody for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Suraj have an excuse ready when he went to his father?
qa.a: He expected shouting and punishment and felt afraid, since his heart was thumping. He was also ashamed of having given the money.

qa.q: What did Suraj's father do that made it easier to confide?
qa.a: He listened without interrupting, thanked him for telling and did not punish him, then went with him to the school.

qa.q: How might Suraj's father have felt hearing the story?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and angry at the older boy but stayed calm, so Suraj would feel safe. 🙂

grounding: A teen confides an unsafe situation to a parent who listens first and stays calm.

passage: I've been the school librarian for eleven years, and I noticed this last week. Kiran stayed behind at closing time, fidgeting with a bookmark, then went to Mrs Sandhu, the counsellor, whose room is next to mine. The door was open a crack. I heard Kiran say something about marks and about not sleeping, and then a pause, and Mrs Sandhu's voice, low and calm. She didn't say 'why did you do that'. She said, 'Tell me more.' I don't know what was said after that. But when Kiran came out, she had the look of someone who has put down something heavy, and she took a book on drawing. Baljeet.

qa.q: What was Kiran fidgeting with at closing time?
qa.a: Kiran was fidgeting with a bookmark.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been feeling when she stayed behind and fidgeted?
qa.a: She may have been nervous and worried about her marks and sleep, and unsure whether to speak. Baljeet adds that he doesn't know what was said after that.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped Kiran open up?
qa.a: She stayed calm, didn't blame, and said 'Tell me more' to invite Kiran to keep talking.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt afterwards?
qa.a: She looked relieved, like someone who had put down something heavy.

grounding: A teen confides stress to a counsellor who listens calmly, seen by a librarian.

passage: At two in the morning in Singapore, Chen typed a long post about how much she hated school, how her parents were being unfair and how she felt like nobody understood her. She added the name of her school and a photo of her uniform. Her thumb hovered over 'Post'. She messaged her friend Oskar: 'Should I put this up?' He replied at once, 'Wait until morning. And take out the school name, strangers can see that.' Chen put the phone face-down. In the morning she deleted the school name and the photo and read the post again. It felt too raw now. She sent it privately to Oskar instead, and they talked at recess about what was actually bothering her.

qa.q: What did Chen add to the post besides her feelings?
qa.a: She added the name of her school and a photo of her uniform.

qa.q: Why was Chen tempted to post at two in the morning?
qa.a: She felt misunderstood and wanted someone to hear how she felt, and the late hour made her feelings seem larger. She may also have wanted attention or support.

qa.q: What worked about Oskar's advice?
qa.a: He told her to wait until morning, take out identifying details and then talk to him, which let her pause and choose a trusted audience.

qa.q: How might her parents have felt if they had seen the post?
qa.a: They may have felt hurt and worried, and it could have made the conversation harder.

grounding: A teen pauses before posting personal details and feelings, and turns to a trusted friend instead.

passage: Mr Francis wrote on the whiteboard: 'What would you never post?' and gave the class of Year Ten two minutes. Samir, who had posted his home address and a photo of his door key ring the week before to show off a new lock, went quiet. Someone said, 'Your address.' Someone else said, 'When you're really upset.' Francis asked the class, 'If it stays online for years, who might see it?' Samir put his hand up slowly. "Someone could read my old posts when I apply for a course." After class he stayed. "I want to delete the address one. Can you help?" Francis nodded. "Let's do it now. And who would you talk to for the big stuff?" Samir thought. "My cousin."

qa.q: What did Mr Francis write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: He wrote: 'What would you never post?'

qa.q: What was Samir probably feeling when he went quiet?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and worried, because he had posted his address and key ring photo, and the discussion made him see the risk. Asking to delete it shows he wanted to fix it.

qa.q: What small step helped Samir?
qa.a: He asked his teacher to help him delete the post right away and named his cousin as someone to talk to about heavy topics.

qa.q: How might Mr Francis have felt when Samir stayed after class?
qa.a: He may have felt pleased that the lesson reached Samir and that Samir trusted him with the problem.

grounding: A teen learns to consider permanence and audience, and uses trusted people for heavy topics, in a class.

passage: Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Chinmay came in to talk about a group project, but after a few minutes he said, laughing, "Sir, hypothetically, if a person wanted to tell somebody they liked them but not really tell them, how would that work?" I asked if he wanted to say more. He shrugged, still smiling, but his knee was bouncing. He told me a girl in his class had smiled at him in the library and he had made a joke about her handwriting, hoping to see what she would say. She laughed and said 'you're silly'. He can't tell whether that was a yes or a no. We talked about telling someone who has been kind and respectful. Thomas.

qa.q: What did Chinmay ask, in a joking way, during the session?
qa.a: He asked how a person could tell someone they liked them without really telling them.

qa.q: What might Chinmay's smile and bouncing knee suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was nervous and half-serious about his question, so the joke may have been covering real feeling. The smile could also just be how he talks about it.

qa.q: What could Chinmay try next?
qa.a: He could share his feelings with someone who has shown care and respect, perhaps a friend first, and be ready to accept whatever answer comes.

qa.q: How might the girl in the library have understood his joke about her handwriting?
qa.a: She may have taken it as friendly teasing, or as a puzzling remark, which is why 'you're silly' is hard to read.

grounding: A teenager hints at a feeling by joking to test the response, and vulnerability is risky.

passage:
Thursday night.

Today in music class I dedicated a song to 'a person in this room who knows who she is'. Everyone laughed and looked around. Dolma looked at her desk. Her face went a bit pink, or maybe that was the light. I don't know what it meant. After class Sahil, my friend, said I'd been too obvious, and I said I was only joking.

But honestly? I wasn't joking, and I felt sick when nobody said anything. I don't want to make her uncomfortable. I think next time I might tell my cousin first, because she's kind and has never laughed at me. Or ask Dolma something normal and see how she treats me.

qa.q: What did Sahil dedicate in music class?
qa.a: He dedicated a song to 'a person in this room who knows who she is'.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling after nobody said anything?
qa.a: He felt sick and unsure, since he had been half-joking to test the response but really meant it. He also worried about making Dolma uncomfortable.

qa.q: What would you advise Sahil to do next?
qa.a: Share the feeling first with someone kind who has never laughed at him and be ready to accept Dolma's answer, whatever it is.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt in the classroom?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised or put on the spot, since she looked at her desk and went pink, though it could also be embarrassment for another reason.

grounding: A teen partially reveals a feeling in a joking way to test the response.

passage:
Wednesday.

Recess was brilliant today. Our group has this running joke about Mr Menon's 'seven-minute stories' that go on for twenty. Farhan does the voice, Aman does the hand gestures, and by the end I was crying with laughter. Naveen joined us last week and stood at the edge not laughing. I think he hasn't got the reference. I felt bad, so I explained it to him. Then someone made a joke about Naveen's accent, and everybody laughed except him. I laughed a second too long and then stopped. His face went closed.

I'm going to tell the boys tomorrow that accent jokes aren't funny, and I'll say sorry to Naveen. 😕

qa.q: What is the group's running joke about?
qa.a: It is about Mr Menon's 'seven-minute stories' that go on for twenty.

qa.q: What was Naveen probably feeling when everyone laughed at the accent joke?
qa.a: He probably felt excluded and hurt, since his face went closed and he didn't laugh. He was also already standing at the edge.

qa.q: What would you advise Farhan to do about the accent jokes?
qa.a: Tell the group calmly that jokes about someone's accent are unkind, and apologise to Naveen for laughing.

qa.q: How might the other boys see the accent joke?
qa.a: They may think it was harmless fun, without noticing how it landed on someone new.

grounding: Banter builds belonging but can exclude, and jokes about someone's accent can harm.

passage:
Monday. Parul made a meme of the school timetable with the caption 'Now with 12 periods of Sanskrit, so we can finally relax' and posted it in the class group. Fifteen people reacted with laughing faces.
Wednesday. Harish asked her at recess, slightly worried, "Is the Sanskrit thing real? My mother asked me." Parul stared at him. "It's a joke, Harish." He said, "It looked like a notice."
Saturday. Parul reposted the meme with a small line at the bottom: 'satire, not a real timetable'. Harish sent her a thumbs-up. She also took down a second meme she'd started that made fun of a boy's stammer. "That one's punching down," she told herself.

qa.q: How many people reacted to Parul's timetable meme?
qa.a: Fifteen people reacted with laughing faces.

qa.q: Why was Harish worried on Wednesday?
qa.a: He thought the meme might be a real notice, and his mother was asking him about it. He may also have felt embarrassed at being fooled.

qa.q: What did Parul do that made her memes safer?
qa.a: She added a label saying it was satire and removed the meme that mocked a boy's stammer.

qa.q: How might the boy with the stammer have felt if the second meme had been posted?
qa.a: He would probably have felt hurt and exposed, since it would have mocked something he cannot help.

grounding: Memes and satire convey shared attitudes economically, may be mistaken for fact, and can hurt if they mock vulnerable people.

passage: Keerthana, my mother used to say a joke has a direction, up or down. When I was young, our neighbourhood theatre group performed a street play where a tiny clerk mocked the corrupt officer, and the whole lane laughed until they wept. That was aimed up, at power. Then a group of boys drew a cartoon of the tea seller's limp and passed it around. That was aimed down, at someone who couldn't answer. I felt sick, though I laughed once, I'm ashamed to say. Today your memes are quicker, but the question stays the same: who is it laughing at, and can they take it? Also, put a note if it's satire, because not everyone knows. Ayesha.

qa.q: What did the tiny clerk do in the street play?
qa.a: He mocked the corrupt officer.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel about the cartoon of the tea seller?
qa.a: She felt sick, and ashamed that she had laughed once, because the joke was aimed at someone who could not answer. It was mockery of a vulnerable person.

qa.q: What two questions does Ayesha suggest asking about a meme?
qa.a: Who the meme is laughing at, and whether that person can take it, plus adding a note when it is satire.

qa.q: How might the tea seller have felt about the cartoon?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt and embarrassed that people made fun of his limp.

grounding: An elder contrasts satire aimed at power with mockery of a vulnerable person, warning satire can be misread.

passage: Sudha's phone buzzed on the desk during study hour. Tanvir had sent, 'Great, just great,' after she'd told him the bus would be late for the fourth time that week. She stared at the flat words. No emoji. Was he angry with her? Frustrated with the bus? Making a joke? Sudha remembered how Tanvir talked when he was cheerful, an actual bounce, and when he was sarcastic, a low flat drawl. In text she could not hear it. Her thumbs hovered. She typed, 'Are you joking or actually upset?' Tanvir replied a minute later, 'ha, both. Bus is late and I'm going to miss cricket.' She sent back a sympathetic face and said she'd wait with him.

qa.q: What did Tanvir send after hearing about the bus?
qa.a: He sent, 'Great, just great,'.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have felt when he sent that message?
qa.a: He was likely frustrated about the late bus and missing cricket, and possibly a little joking too, as he said 'both'. Sudha could not tell from the flat words alone.

qa.q: What made Sudha's question helpful?
qa.a: She asked directly whether he was joking or upset, so she didn't assume contempt or humour from flat text.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt if Sudha had assumed he was angry with her?
qa.a: He may have felt misunderstood and defensive, since his frustration was about the bus. 🙂

grounding: Sarcasm can signal frustration, humour or contempt, and in text a clarifying question is fair.

passage:
"Great, just great," said Sangeeta, flatly, dropping her bag as the rain came through the ceiling of the practice room.
"Are you joking?" Gopika asked, looking up from the drum.
"Am I laughing?"
"No. So you're annoyed?"
Sangeeta let out a breath. "Yes. We booked this room a month ago and now the rehearsal's off."
"Okay, that's a real problem. I thought maybe you were teasing me for being late."
"No, I was being sarcastic at the roof." Sangeeta almost smiled. "Sorry, I sound like a villain when I'm cross."
"There's the church hall down the street," Gopika said. "Want to ask?"

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta drop her bag?
qa.a: She was annoyed because the rain was coming through the ceiling of the practice room.

qa.q: Why did Gopika ask whether Sangeeta was joking?
qa.a: She could not tell whether the flat 'great, just great' meant humour, frustration or teasing about her being late, and she did not want to guess wrong. Her worry about being teased shows the doubt.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that helped after Sangeeta explained?
qa.a: She acknowledged the problem and suggested asking at the church hall, turning the annoyance into a next step.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta's tone sound to someone who didn't know her?
qa.a: It could sound like contempt or anger at the person, which is why a check like Gopika's is fair.

grounding: Sarcasm with flat delivery is easily misread, and a clarifying question resolves it.
